HYTI: Treasury securities paired with an options strategy on high yield corporate bonds, selling call options to manufacture a target income stream. Instead of owning junk bonds directly, it harvests option premiums, so the payout depends on bond market volatility as much as on interest.
VCHY: High yield corporate bonds from hundreds of US borrowers, cruise lines, satellite firms, health care companies and more, each capped so no issuer dominates. It is a plain, broad junk bond holding built for income, with the usual warning that these borrowers default more often in recessions.
CNXT: The 100 largest companies on China's ChiNext board in Shenzhen, the country's startup-heavy exchange: battery makers, optical network gear, solar and medical firms, with technology over half. It is a focused bet on Chinese innovation, and ChiNext stocks are known for especially sharp price swings.
RCGE: Companies around the world chosen for a demonstrated commitment to gender balance in management and across their workforce, spread across finance, consumer brands, health care and industry. It is a values-screened global core holding, so the equality commitment, not sector bets, is what sets it apart.
PBQQ: Four Nasdaq-100 buffer funds layered together, each with its own one-year protection period starting a quarter apart, so part of the fund resets every three months. The ladder smooths the timing risk of a single reset date while keeping a buffer against a first slice of losses.
QUIZ: Quality companies in developed markets outside the US, chosen by Zacks for strong fundamentals, with banks the biggest slice at nearly a third. It is a core international holding with a quality filter, favoring steady earners in Europe and Japan over speculative names.
BNDS: A high income mix that is half bonds and half preferred shares, leaning on energy and financial issuers that pay generous distributions. Preferred shares sit between stocks and bonds in risk, so the fund chases yield well beyond a core bond fund, with bigger price swings to match.
LDRC: A ladder of corporate bond funds that each mature in a set year, spread evenly from 2027 through 2031, then rolled forward as years pass. Laddering spreads interest rate risk across maturities, giving a steadier, more predictable version of short-term corporate bond income.
DIEM: Emerging market stocks tilted to pay a higher dividend yield than the broad developing-world market, though Asian chipmakers still make technology the biggest slice at over two-fifths. It blends income with emerging market growth, favoring payers in Taiwan, Korea, Brazil and beyond.
RFLR: US small company stocks paired with an options floor designed to limit how far the fund can fall over each period. Small caps offer growth with rough swings, and the managed floor aims to soften the worst of them, giving up some upside for the brake.
SPBX: Six large-cap buffer funds layered together, each running a six-month protection period starting a month apart, each absorbing the first 10 percent of losses for its slice. A new slice resets every month, spreading timing risk while the buffers trade away gains past caps.
XBJA: Options on large US stocks with a twist: gains are amplified up to a cap, while a buffer (the 9 in its name) absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each January. It is a leveraged-feeling but bounded bet for investors expecting a decent, not spectacular, year.
BAMD: Dividend-paying US stocks picked by active managers, led by banks and financial firms at about a quarter, with energy, technology and household brands behind. It is built for income from established payers rather than growth names, so the payout stream matters more than price fireworks.
VEGA: A global mix of stock, bond and commodity funds with covered call options sold against the holdings, a strategy called buy-write. The option premiums add income and cushion small declines, at the cost of capping gains, making it a steadier, income-leaning way to hold world markets.
GOP: Stocks that Republican members of Congress and their families have reported buying, copied from public disclosure filings. It is a mirror of politicians' own portfolios, heavy in technology and industry, and it sets itself apart by following the money of one party's lawmakers.
FXA: Actual Australian dollars held in a deposit account, packaged as a stock so investors can hold the currency in a brokerage account. It simply rises and falls with the Australian dollar, making it a direct currency bet tied to interest rates and commodity-rich Australia's economy.
VCOB: Core US bonds actively managed: Treasuries, government mortgage bonds and corporate debt, chosen for a mix of interest income and price gains. Active management sets it apart from index bond funds, with managers shifting maturities and credit as they hunt for value.
QMAG: Options on the Nasdaq-100, the big technology and internet companies, with a moderate cushion that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each August. It softens one of the market's most growth-heavy indexes, trading away some upside for a calmer ride.
GISC: Securitized debt: bonds backed by home mortgages, commercial property loans and other pooled borrowing, actively selected across the securitized market. It aims for income with risks that differ from corporate bonds, since repayment depends on thousands of underlying borrowers rather than single companies.
VUSV: Large US value stocks actively picked by Wellington Management, spread evenly across finance, technology, health care and industry. Vanguard pairs its low-key index heritage with active stock picking here, favoring companies priced below their worth, including some big tech names value funds usually skip.
JANB: Options giving structured exposure to large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to cushion losses over an outcome period that resets each January. The Aptus design trades gains past a cap for a buffer, aiming for stock market participation with a calmer ride.
JMMF: A money market fund holding only US Treasury bills, notes and bonds, the safest corner of the cash world. Investors use it to park money with government backing and daily liquidity, earning a modest yield while aiming to keep a steady one-dollar share price.
NORW: Companies of Norway, one country's whole market: oil and gas producers are about a third, with banks, salmon farming, shipping and defense firms behind. It is a single-country bet on a wealthy, energy-rich economy, so oil prices and the krone steer results.
FGM: German companies selected by a quantitative AlphaDEX scoring system rather than by size, which tilts it toward mid-sized industrial, airline, materials and drug firms. It offers Germany exposure beyond the usual giant exporters, with stock selection, not the broad market, driving results.
MAVF: Large US companies their managers judge undervalued, which in practice includes many big technology names alongside banks and consumer firms. It is an active value fund willing to buy growth stocks when they look cheap, so its lineup often resembles a blend fund more than a classic value portfolio.
SEPQ: A tactical mix that rotates among big Nasdaq-listed growth stocks, long-term Treasury bonds and cash-like Treasury bills as conditions change. It aims to lean into growth when markets cooperate and shelter in bonds and cash when they do not, a flexibility plain stock funds lack.
HUMN: Companies building humanoid robots and their parts: robot makers in China, Japan and Korea, the precision gears and joints inside them, and carmakers developing their own machines. It is an early-stage, concentrated bet that human-shaped robots become a real industry, so expect sharp swings.
PRXG: Large US growth companies screened to align with the manager's stewardship values, though technology giants still dominate at nearly three-fifths of the fund. It pairs mainstream growth exposure with a values filter, which can exclude or favor companies on more than financial grounds.
IBIK: Inflation-protected US Treasury bonds, called TIPS, all maturing in 2034, whose principal rises with inflation. Because every bond matures the same year, it works like buying one inflation-proof bond: hold to 2034 and the inflation adjustment is locked in, while prices swing before then.
DDSQ: Built to gain from moves in either direction over each quarterly period: it can profit when large US stocks fall modestly as well as when they rise, up to a cap. The 5 in its name is the buffer against deeper losses, and the design resets every three months.
LOEV: A select portfolio of companies in developed markets outside the US, banks, oil, insurers and industrial leaders across Europe and Japan, picked for quality and growth at reasonable prices. Harding Loevner's managers hold a focused list with patience, so stock picking drives results.
THYP: A single cryptocurrency, HYPE, the token of the Hyperliquid trading platform, with part of the holdings staked, meaning locked up to support the network in exchange for extra tokens. Staking adds yield to a pure price bet, though the token itself can swing violently.
NATO: Defense companies headquartered in NATO member countries: American and European makers of fighter jets, missiles, warships and aircraft engines, nearly all industrial firms. It is a transatlantic bet on rising military budgets across the alliance, tied to geopolitics rather than consumer demand.
KLIP: Chinese internet companies, online shopping, social media, gaming and delivery platforms, with covered call options sold against the position for income. The calls generate a payout stream from a famously volatile sector, at the cost of giving up part of any sharp rebound.
FRNW: Clean energy companies worldwide: wind turbine makers, solar firms, renewable power producers and the utilities buying their output, with utilities the biggest slice at nearly half. It is a broad bet on the shift from fossil fuels, spanning both the builders and the operators of green power.
PRMR: An actively managed, frequently traded portfolio of large US companies, spread across technology, finance, consumer and health care names. Frequent trading sets it apart from buy-and-hold funds: the managers act on shorter-term signals, so the lineup and results can change character quickly.
AVMA: A balanced mix of other Avantis funds, roughly two-thirds stocks from around the world and one-third bonds, all tilted toward cheaper and more profitable companies. It is a one-fund moderate portfolio for hands-off investors, with the factor tilts setting it apart from plain balanced funds.
AFGR: Large US growth companies picked by several specialist management teams working side by side, with technology over half the fund. Using multiple managers is the point: it blends different stock-picking styles into one growth fund, softening the risk of any single team being wrong.
BCIL: Large companies outside the US chosen one by one by active managers, an eclectic mix from Polish gym chains to Australian electronics retailers and Korean chipmakers. With no index to hug, results rest entirely on the managers' picks, making it a conviction-driven international growth fund.
DWAW: A world fund of funds guided by Dorsey Wright's momentum research, rotating among stock factor funds from many countries, with the freedom to retreat into short-term bonds and cash. That defensive gear sets it apart: at times it can sit mostly in cash-like holdings.
PSMR: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged under a structured outcome design that cushions a middle range of losses over a period resetting each April. It trades some upside for that moderate protection, aiming for a calmer ride than owning stocks outright.
NMAR: Options on the Nasdaq-100, the big technology and internet companies, with a power buffer that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each March. It is built for investors who want growth-stock exposure with a shock absorber, accepting capped gains in return.
SMAX: Options on large US stocks arranged for the maximum buffer in its family over a year running from September, built to shield against nearly the whole of a market drop. That near-total protection comes with a modest cap, so it suits capital preservation more than growth.
FCUS: A focused portfolio of mid-sized US growth companies, with memory chip and data storage makers leading a technology slice of nearly three-quarters. Such concentration means a single industry's fortunes, especially the memory cycle, can drive the whole fund's results.
SPBW: Twelve large-cap buffer funds layered together, each running its own one-year period starting a month apart, each absorbing the first 20 percent of losses for its slice. A slice resets every month, so protection is always fresh somewhere in the fund, with gains capped in exchange.
PRXV: Large US value companies screened to align with the manager's stewardship values, spread across banks, health care, technology and consumer brands. It pairs dividend-leaning value exposure with a values filter, which shapes the lineup beyond the usual cheapness and profitability tests.
FXB: Actual British pounds held in a deposit account, packaged as a stock so investors can hold the currency in a brokerage account. It simply rises and falls with the pound, making it a direct bet on Britain's currency, steered by interest rates and the UK economy.
STNC: US companies that meet the manager's sustainability standards, spread across technology, health care, consumer and industrial firms in roughly equal measure. It is an actively managed core stock fund with a green screen, favoring established businesses rather than speculative clean-tech names.
AGNG: Companies serving the world's aging population: drugmakers, medical device firms, health insurers and the owners of senior housing and care facilities, mostly in health care. It is a demographic bet on longer lives needing more medicine and care, steadier than most theme funds.
PCLG: A focused portfolio of about two dozen large companies with durable competitive advantages, picked by Polen Capital for steady, compounding growth. Concentration is the point: software, payments and chip leaders dominate, and each holding is expected to earn its place for years.
